mmt-be-01-010:
Interviewers ask how you design objects that cannot change after construction, and why that helps concurrent systems.

An immutable class has all fields private final, no setters, a constructor (or factory) that fully initializes state, and defensive copies for mutable inputs/outputs (e.g. clone a Date or wrap with List.copyOf). Mark the class final (or use a record in Java 16+) so subclasses cannot reintroduce mutability. All methods must not mutate fields.

Why it matters for concurrency: once published, immutable objects need no locks — they are inherently thread-safe for reads. Multiple booking/payment threads can share a Money, FareQuote, or itinerary DTO without races. Prefer immutable value objects in caches and event payloads so Redis/Kafka consumers never see half-updated state.

Follow-ups / pitfalls: shallow immutability (mutable field still shared); publishing this from the constructor; confusing final reference with immutable contents; records use accessors like x(), not getX().
mmt-be-01-011:
The question checks whether you understand that generics are largely a compile-time feature in Java.

Type erasure means the compiler checks and inserts casts for type parameters, then strips them from bytecode. At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are both raw List. You cannot use new T(), create T[] easily, or check instanceof List<String>. Bridges and synthetic casts preserve type safety after erasure.

When it matters: designing generic repositories, mappers, or response wrappers for booking APIs. You use bounded wildcards (? extends/? super) for PECS, and often pass a Class<T> or TypeReference when frameworks need reified types (Jackson, Redis serializers).

Pitfalls: heap pollution via raw types; assuming runtime generics exist (they do not like C#); overusing wildcards; forgetting that primitive generics need boxing (List<Integer> not List<int> until Valhalla).
mmt-be-01-013:
They want internal structure and complexity trade-offs, not just “ArrayList is array, LinkedList is nodes.”

ArrayList backs data with a contiguous Object array, grows by ~1.5× on resize (amortized O(1) add at end). Random access is O(1); insert/remove in the middle is O(n) due to shifting. Better locality → CPU-cache friendly.

LinkedList is a doubly linked list of nodes (prev/next + item). Mid insert/remove is O(1) if you already hold the node; getting there via index is still O(n). Extra pointer overhead and poor cache locality make it slower for most real workloads.

Travel context: use ArrayList for result lists (search hits, seat maps, fare options). Prefer ArrayDeque over LinkedList for queues/stacks. Almost never choose LinkedList in production Java unless you need frequent splice from known iterators.

Pitfalls: LinkedList for random access; measuring only asymptotic cost and ignoring cache miss cost; using LinkedList as a queue instead of ArrayDeque/ConcurrentLinkedQueue.
mmt-be-01-014:
This tests String internals and reference vs value equality.

Java maintains a string pool (interned strings in the heap). Literals like "DEL" are interned automatically. new String("DEL") creates a distinct heap object. s.intern() returns the pooled instance for that content.

== compares references (same object?). equals() compares character content. Two equal literals usually share a pool entry so == may be true; two constructed strings with same text usually have == false but equals true. Always use equals (or Objects.equals) for content; never rely on == for business strings (PNR, city codes, coupon codes).

Use: pooling saves memory for repeated constants; intern() rarely belongs in hot booking paths — it can contend on the pool.

Pitfalls: using == in auth/token checks; interning unbounded user input (memory leak); confusing pool behavior across JVMs/versions.
mmt-be-01-015:
Candidates often mix up nested classes vs static methods — clarify both.

A static nested class is nested for packaging but does not hold an implicit reference to an outer instance. It can access only static members of the outer class. Use it for helpers tightly coupled to the outer type (e.g. Booking.Builder, Holder idiom for Singleton) without leaking the outer this.

A static method belongs to the class, not an instance — no this, cannot access instance fields. Use for pure utilities, factories (Money.of), or entry points.

When: static nested for Builder/DTO companions; avoid non-static inner classes in long-lived caches/listeners (memory leaks via outer reference). Prefer instance methods when polymorphic behavior or test doubles are needed.

Pitfalls: calling static methods via instances (confusing); overusing static (harder to mock); non-static inner class retaining outer BookingService in a thread pool.
mmt-be-01-016:
They want the Java 8 functional programming building block.

A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM). It may have defaults/statics. Annotate with @FunctionalInterface so the compiler enforces the contract. Lambdas and method references target these types.

Three from java.util.function: Function<T,R> (apply) — map DTO→entity; Predicate<T> (test) — filter available rooms; Consumer<T> (accept) — side effects like metrics. Also know Supplier, BiFunction, UnaryOperator.

Why: Streams, Spring callbacks, CompletableFuture transforms, Strategy-style pricing lambdas without anonymous classes.

Pitfalls: multiple abstract methods break lambdas; checked exceptions inside lambdas are awkward; confusing functional interfaces with “any interface with methods.”
mmt-be-01-017:
Optional (Java 8+) expresses possibly-absent return values without raw nulls.

Use Optional<T> as a return type when absence is a valid outcome: findBookingByPnr, optional add-ons. Prefer Optional.ofNullable, then map/flatMap/orElse/orElseGet/orElseThrow. Do not use Optional for fields, method parameters, or collections elements — that adds allocation and noise. Never store null inside Optional.

Travel use: optional meal preference, missing hotel amenity, soft-fail enrichment from a secondary catalog service — make absence explicit at API boundaries.

Pitfalls: optional.get() without check; orElse(heavy()) evaluating eagerly (use orElseGet); returning Optional from JPA entities; wrapping everything in Optional and still returning null from other methods.
mmt-be-01-019:
They want awareness of scheduling cost when threads ≫ cores.

A CPU core runs one thread (or two with HT) at a time. Extra threads are time-sliced: the OS saves/restores registers, may invalidate cache locality, and incurs context-switch overhead. For CPU-bound work, more threads than cores usually slows throughput. For I/O-bound work (DB, Redis, airline GDS calls), more threads can help hide latency — until queueing, lock contention, and memory (stack ~1MB each) dominate.

Booking systems: size pools for I/O (Tomcat/WebFlux, JDBC pool) separately from CPU pools (ForkJoin for CPU tasks). Prefer async/reactive or bounded executors over unbounded new Thread.

Pitfalls: unbounded thread creation on traffic spikes; equating “more threads = faster”; ignoring that blocking on locks with huge pools amplifies latency.
mmt-be-02-010:
Dependency Injection wires collaborators without hard new — Spring supports three styles.

  • Constructor injection (preferred): required deps as final fields. Immutable, easy to test, fails fast if a bean is missing, works with required args. Spring Boot recommends this.
  • Setter injection: optional dependencies after construction. Mutable; circular deps sometimes “fixed” this way (usually a design smell).
  • Field injection (@Autowired on fields): concise but hides deps, breaks immutability, harder unit tests without Spring, reflection-based.

Travel services: inject PaymentClient, InventoryService via constructors so BookingService is explicit and testable.

Pitfalls: circular dependencies; injecting concrete classes instead of interfaces; mixing field injection with finals; huge constructors (split the class).
mmt-be-02-012:
Profiles activate environment-specific beans and properties.

Define application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml, etc. Activate via spring.profiles.active=prod (env var, JVM arg, or IDE). Annotate beans with @Profile("prod") so e.g. real payment gateway loads only in prod, while sandbox beans load in dev/qa. You can combine profiles and use @ActiveProfiles in tests.

MMT-style use: different Redis/Kafka clusters, feature flags, and GDS credentials per env without code forks.

Pitfalls: forgetting to set active profile in prod (falls back to defaults); secrets in git’d yml instead of env/secret manager; overlapping profile-specific beans causing duplicate definitions.
mmt-be-02-013:
All four are stereotype annotations that mark a class as a Spring-managed component; scanning picks them up.

  • @Component: generic stereotype.
  • @Service: business/application logic (booking orchestration).
  • @Repository: persistence; enables exception translation to DataAccessException.
  • @Controller/@RestController: web layer; maps HTTP to handlers. @RestController = controller + @ResponseBody.

Functionally similar for bean creation; the distinction documents layering and enables AOP pointcuts (e.g. tx around @Service, persistence advice on @Repository).

Pitfalls: putting business logic in controllers; using @Component everywhere and losing clear architecture; forgetting @Repository then missing exception translation.
mmt-be-02-014:
They want the ordered lifecycle of a Spring bean.

Rough flow: instantiate → populate properties/DI → aware interfaces (BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware) → BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization → @PostConstruct / InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet / custom init-method → postProcessAfterInitialization (proxies often wrap here) → bean ready. On shutdown: @PreDestroy / DisposableBean.destroy / custom destroy method.

Use: warm Redis connections, register health checks, start Kafka listeners carefully, flush buffers on destroy.

Pitfalls: heavy work in constructors before DI; relying on @PostConstruct for cross-bean ordering without @DependsOn; forgetting destroy hooks for thread pools (leaks).
mmt-be-02-015:
Spring MVC request flow centers on DispatcherServlet.

Request hits the servlet → HandlerMapping finds a handler (controller method) → HandlerAdapter invokes it (after HandlerInterceptor.preHandle) → controller returns ModelAndView / body → interceptors postHandle → for view-based apps ViewResolver resolves a View and renders; for REST, message converters write JSON → afterCompletion.

Travel APIs: typically @RestController — no JSP ViewResolver; still the same DispatcherServlet pipeline for auth interceptors, logging, and exception handlers (@ControllerAdvice).

Pitfalls: confusing Filters (servlet container) with Interceptors (Spring MVC); assuming ViewResolver always runs for JSON APIs; blocking long GDS calls on the servlet thread without timeouts.
mmt-be-02-017:
Spring Cloud is a toolkit for microservice patterns on Spring Boot: discovery, config, gateway, circuit breakers, etc.

Eureka is a client-server service registry. Services annotate @EnableEurekaClient/@EnableDiscoveryClient, register heartbeat + host/port/metadata. Callers use the logical name (e.g. payment-service) with DiscoveryClient, Ribbon/Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, or OpenFeign instead of hard-coded IPs.

When: classic VM/EC2 microservice fleets. In Kubernetes, prefer native Service DNS + kube-proxy; Eureka is less common unless migrating legacy Spring Cloud stacks.

Pitfalls: treating Eureka as CAP-strong consistency; stale registry after crashes (self-preservation mode); mixing Eureka with K8s without clear ownership of discovery.
mmt-be-03-007:
Pick the communication style based on sync needs, latency, and coupling.

  • REST/HTTP+JSON: human-debuggable, language-agnostic, great for public/BFF APIs (search, booking status). Higher overhead, weaker typing unless OpenAPI.
  • gRPC: protobuf + HTTP/2, multiplexed, low latency, strong contracts. Best for internal sync calls (pricing → inventory) where you control both ends.
  • Queues/Kafka: async, buffer spikes, fan-out. Use for booking confirmations, notifications, payment webhooks processing, inventory sync — when the caller should not block on downstream.

Rule of thumb: user waits → REST/gRPC with timeouts + CB; fire-and-forget / eventual → queue. Avoid chatty sync webs of services for a single booking click.

Pitfalls: using Kafka for request/response RPC; no idempotency on consumers; REST without timeouts.
mmt-be-03-012:
Consistency models describe when all replicas/readers agree on the latest write.

Strong consistency: after a write commits, every subsequent read sees it (or fails). Needed for payments, seat inventory, wallet balances — double-bookings and double-charges are unacceptable.

Eventual consistency: replicas converge over time; interim stale reads allowed. Fine for hotel content, review counts, “recently viewed,” search indexes, loyalty point displays with delayed credit.

When to sacrifice strong consistency: cross-region scale, availability under partition (AP in CAP), read-heavy catalogs. Mitigate with versioning, read-your-writes for the booking user, and clear UX (“confirmation pending”).

Pitfalls: caching strongly consistent data without invalidation; assuming Kafka consumers imply strong consistency across services.
mmt-be-03-013:
Distributed transactions need patterns because a single DB ACID TX cannot span services.

  • 2PC: prepare then commit across resources. Strong, but blocking, poorly scalable, coordinator SPOF — rarely used across microservices.
  • Saga: sequence of local txs with compensations (release seat if payment fails). Orchestration or choreography.
  • Transactional Outbox: write business row + outbox event in one local TX; a relay publishes to Kafka. Avoids “DB committed but event lost.” Pair with inbox/idempotent consumers.

Booking flow: reserve inventory → charge → confirm; outbox emits BookingConfirmed; compensations unwind on failure.

Pitfalls: saga without idempotent steps; dual-write (DB then Kafka without outbox); long 2PC locks under GDS latency.
mmt-be-03-014:
An API Gateway is the single entry for clients into many backends.

It typically handles: routing, TLS termination, authn (JWT validation), rate limiting, request logging, aggregation/BFF shaping, canary routing, and protocol translation. Microservices keep domain logic: booking rules, pricing, inventory, payments.

Travel: mobile/web hit gateway → route to search, booking, trips services; gateway enforces API keys/OAuth and shields internal mesh.

Pitfalls: stuffing business logic into the gateway; gateway as bottleneck without horizontal scale; duplicating auth in every service and ignoring zero-trust internals.
mmt-be-03-015:
In Kubernetes, service discovery is mostly platform-native.

Pods get ephemeral IPs. You expose a Service (ClusterIP/headless) with a stable DNS name payment.default.svc.cluster.local. kube-proxy or eBPF (Cilium) load-balances to ready endpoints from Endpoints/EndpointSlices. Health probes remove bad pods. For multi-cluster/mesh, use Istio/Linkerd for mTLS and advanced routing; optionally an external registry for hybrid legacy.

Vs Eureka: prefer K8s DNS + Services unless you must keep Spring Cloud Netflix. Clients call logical service names; avoid hard-coding pod IPs.

Pitfalls: missing readiness probes (traffic to starting pods); relying on client-side caching of IPs; mixing Eureka heartbeats with K8s without dual registration plan.
mmt-be-03-016:
Fill this STAR for your interview (example scenario: flash-sale flight inventory).

Situation: During a sale, search/hold APIs hammered MySQL for seat maps; cache stampedes and async confirmation lags caused timeouts and duplicate holds. [Your system/year].

Task: Cut p99 latency and eliminate double-holds under spike traffic while keeping booking correctness.

Action — Redis: Cache-aside seat-map/fare snapshots with short TTL; distributed lock / SET NX for hold keys; rate-limit buckets per user; stampede protection (single-flight / probabilistic early expire).

Action — Kafka: Publish HoldCreated/PaymentCaptured via outbox; consumers update inventory projections and notify; idempotent keys on PNR/holdId; partition by flightId for ordering.

Result: Fill metrics — e.g. p99 ___ → ___ ms, DB QPS −___%, zero duplicate holds in ___ days, consumer lag < ___ s. Tie to dashboards you owned.

Follow-ups: eviction policy, exactly-once vs idempotent at-least-once, poison messages, why not only Redis or only Kafka.
mmt-be-04-007:
Trivia with a systems-thinking follow-up: MongoDB’s core server is written primarily in C++ (with some JS for server-side scripting historically, and other languages in the ecosystem/tools/drivers).

Why interviewers ask: it signals you know Mongo is a native, performance-oriented database engine—not a JVM app. Memory management, WiredTiger storage, and concurrency live in C++ land; your Java driver is a client talking BSON over the wire.

Why it matters in practice: tuning (cache, WiredTiger, indexes) and failure modes are server-side; language of the DB ≠ language of your Spring service. Choose Mongo for flexible hotel content documents; don’t expect JVM tooling to “see inside” the engine beyond metrics/logs.

Pitfall: confusing MongoDB (C++) with the shell/driver languages, or assuming “NoSQL = slow scripting language DB.”
mmt-be-04-008:
Design a normalized relational model for railway ticketing with clear concurrency boundaries.

  • Train: train_no, name, type.
  • Station: code, name.
  • Route/Schedule: train_id, station_id, seq, arrival, departure, day_offset — ordered path.
  • Coach/Seat inventory: run_date, train_id, coach, seat_no, status (AVAILABLE/HELD/BOOKED), version for optimistic lock.
  • Booking: pnr, user_id, status, amount, created_at.
  • Booking_Passenger / Booking_Seat: links passengers to specific seats for a date; segment from_station→to_station.

Inventory is per train + date; booking must atomically transition seats. Segment occupancy: a seat is free for A→C only if no overlapping booked segment.

Pitfalls: storing only city pairs without sequence; no version/lock; denormalizing seat status into booking only (races).
mmt-be-04-009:
They want raw SQL thinking on graph-like station connectivity via route tables.

Given route(train_id, station_id, seq), trains from A to B:

SELECT r1.train_id FROM route r1 JOIN route r2 ON r1.train_id = r2.train_id WHERE r1.station_id = :from AND r2.station_id = :to AND r1.seq < r2.seq;

Add schedule joins for time windows; for one stop change, self-join two train legs on an intermediate station with timing constraints (arrival before departure). Prefer recursive CTEs or a precomputed connectivity table for multi-hop.

Indexes: (station_id, train_id, seq) and (train_id, seq).

Pitfalls: forgetting seq order (wrong direction); ORM hiding bad Cartesian joins; computing multi-hop solely in app without limits.
mmt-be-04-012:
Query optimisation starts with measuring via EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

Look for: type=ALL (full scan), high rows examined vs returned, temporary tables/filesorts, missing ref/range access. Fix with selective indexes matching WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY. A covering index includes all needed columns so InnoDB can answer from the index alone.

InnoDB detail: secondary indexes store the indexed columns + primary key; PK lookups may need a second hop to the clustered index unless covering.

Travel: index (from, to, travel_date) for search; avoid functions on columns; paginate with keyset not huge OFFSET.

Pitfalls: indexing low-cardinality flags; too many indexes slowing writes; SELECT * preventing covering plans.
mmt-be-04-013:
Normalisation structures data to reduce redundancy (1NF→3NF/BCNF): separate trains, stations, bookings, payments with FKs. Improves integrity and update consistency.

Denormalise when read latency/scale dominate: store city names on booking rows for history, maintain a search document with embedded fare bands, or a Redis projection of seat maps. Accept controlled duplication + sync strategy (events/CDC).

MMT: payments/bookings stay normalized+ACID; hotel catalog and search results often denormalized/NoSQL for nested variability and fast reads.

Pitfalls: denormalising without invalidation; over-normalising hot read paths into excessive joins; updating only one copy of duplicated data.
mmt-be-04-017:
Cache stampede (thundering herd): many requests miss an expired hot key simultaneously and all hit the DB.

Mitigations: (1) single-flight / mutex — only one thread rebuilds the key, others wait; (2) probabilistic early expiration — refresh before TTL randomly; (3) stale-while-revalidate — serve stale briefly while refreshing; (4) cache warming for top routes; (5) slightly jittered TTLs.

Travel: popular DEL-BOM fares or hotel rate caches expiring together during evening peaks.

Pitfalls: locking without timeout (deadlock); infinite TTL without invalidation; stampede on empty results (cache negative lookups with short TTL).
mmt-be-05-007:
Both coordinate access to shared resources; ownership differs.

A mutex is a binary lock owned by one thread: lock/unlock for exclusive critical sections (update in-memory seat map). Unlock only by owner.

A semaphore is a counter of permits: acquire/release by any thread. Binary semaphore ≈ mutex but without ownership semantics. Counting semaphore limits concurrency (e.g. max 50 parallel GDS connections, DB pool style).

Use mutex for mutual exclusion; semaphore for rate/capacity limiting and producer-consumer slots.

Pitfalls: using semaphore as mutex and releasing from wrong thread; forgetting release in finally; confusing fairness policies.
mmt-be-05-008:
The critical section problem: design entry/exit protocols so at most one process executes shared code at a time, with progress and bounded waiting (no deadlock/starvation).

Peterson’s algorithm (two processes): each sets a flag that it wants to enter and sets turn to the other; a process waits while the other wants in and turn is the other. Guarantees mutual exclusion using only shared memory (software solution for 2 processes). Modern systems use hardware atomics / OS locks instead, but Peterson shows the theory.

Interview angle: relate to Java synchronized/locks solving the same problem with stronger progress guarantees on multiprocessors (memory model).

Pitfalls: claiming Peterson scales easily to N processes (needs generalizations); ignoring memory ordering on real CPUs.
mmt-be-05-009:
Java offers multiple synchronisation tools — pick by use case.

  • synchronized: intrinsic monitor; simple critical sections, reentrant.
  • ReentrantLock: explicit lock with tryLock, fairness option, multiple conditions — better for timed booking locks.
  • CountDownLatch: one-shot wait until N events complete (wait for N fare providers).
  • Semaphore: permit counting for concurrency limits.

Also know CyclicBarrier, ReadWriteLock, and java.util.concurrent.atomic for lock-free counters.

Pitfalls: synchronized on public API objects; latch reuse (use CyclicBarrier/Phaser); forgetting unlock in finally.
mmt-be-05-010:
CPU cache memory stores recently used data/instructions closer than RAM to hide DRAM latency.

  • L1: smallest/fastest, per-core (instr+data).
  • L2: larger, usually per-core.
  • L3: shared across cores on a socket, larger/slower than L1/L2.

Misses cascade to the next level then RAM. Matters because contiguous ArrayList scans beat pointer-chasing LinkedLists; false sharing of adjacent fields on different cores hurts throughput. Hot booking loops and serialization benefit from locality.

Pitfalls: confusing CPU cache with Redis; ignoring false sharing on padded counters.
mmt-be-05-013:
Map common protocols to layers (OSI vs TCP/IP mental model).

  • L7 Application: HTTP/HTTPS, gRPC, DNS, SMTP, Kafka app protocol.
  • L6 Presentation: TLS encryption/encoding (often discussed with L7).
  • L5 Session: less explicit in TCP/IP; sessions at app (JWT/cookies).
  • L4 Transport: TCP, UDP.
  • L3 Network: IP, ICMP, routing.
  • L2 Data Link: Ethernet, MAC, switches.
  • L1 Physical: cables, signalling.

Load balancers may operate L4 (TCP) or L7 (HTTP path routing) — important for API gateway design.

Pitfall: saying HTTPS is only L4; TLS is above TCP.
mmt-be-05-014:
Secure APIs with defence in depth.

  • Transport: HTTPS/TLS only; HSTS.
  • Authn/Authz: OAuth2/JWT or mTLS for service-to-service; least-privilege roles on booking/payment endpoints.
  • Rate limiting & WAF: per-IP/user/API-key to stop brute force and scraping of fares.
  • Input validation: schema validation, reject unexpected fields, parameterized SQL, output encoding.
  • Other: idempotency keys for payments, secrets in vault, audit logs, CORS lockdown, dependency scanning.

Pitfalls: putting secrets in JWTs without encryption needs; no token expiry/revocation strategy; trusting only gateway auth for internal lateral movement.
mmt-be-06-001:
Singleton ensures one instance — must be thread-safe under concurrent getInstance.

Initialization-on-demand Holder: private constructor; static nested Holder with static final INSTANCE. JVM class loading initializes the holder lazily and thread-safely without synchronized on every call. Preferred lazy Singleton.

Enum Singleton: enum E { INSTANCE } — concise, serialization-safe, resistant to reflection attacks. Great for stateless utilities (config facade).

When: shared clients (metrics registry) — but prefer DI singletons in Spring over hand-rolled ones.

Pitfalls: double-checked locking without volatile; eager static init hiding errors; Singleton carrying mutable global booking state (hard tests).
mmt-be-06-002:
State Pattern replaces big conditionals with state objects that define behavior and transitions.

For a vending machine (MMT classic): states like Idle → (insertCoin) → HasMoney → (selectItem) → Dispensing → Idle; invalid ops are no-ops or errors inside the state. Context (VendingMachine) holds current state and delegates insertCoin/selectItem/dispense.

Travel analogue: booking lifecycle CREATED→HELD→PAID→CONFIRMED→CANCELLED with legal transitions only.

Follow-ups: thread safety of transitions; persisting state; vs Strategy (algorithms vs lifecycle).

Pitfall: putting all transition logic back into the context class.
mmt-be-06-006:
Factory Method lets a creator return products via an interface without exposing construction. Abstract Factory groups related factories (families of products).

Production uses: payment gateway factory (Razorpay/Paytm/Card clients by country); notification channel factory (email/SMS/push); Spring’s BeanFactory/converter factories. Abstract Factory when you need matching families (e.g. PDF + Email templates per brand).

Why: open/closed — add providers without switching on enums everywhere.

Pitfalls: factory explosion; Abstract Factory when a simple Strategy/map of beans suffices; hiding DI behind static factories.
mmt-be-06-009:
Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind an interface; context selects one at runtime.

Example: PricingStrategy with BaseFare, SurgePricing, CouponPricing, CorporateNegotiated. Booking service holds a strategy (or list of decorators) and computes payable amount without if-else chains. Spring: inject Map<String, PricingStrategy> beans keyed by code.

When: fares, cancellation penalties, tax engines that change by airline/hotel/market.

Vs State: Strategy swaps algorithms; State swaps behavior based on lifecycle. Pitfall: strategies with hidden shared mutable state.
mmt-be-06-010:
Chain of Responsibility passes a request along handlers until one processes it (or each does partial work).

Classic cash denomination: handlers for 500→200→100→50 notes each take what they can and forward remainder. Pipelines: auth → validation → enrichment → rate-limit for booking requests; each handler calls next.

Spring: filter/interceptor chains embody this idea.

Pitfalls: broken chain (null next); order bugs; using CoR when a simple ordered list/loop is clearer; handlers with side effects and no clear contract.
mmt-be-06-011:
Interceptor Pattern inserts cross-cutting logic around a core invocation without modifying it.

In Spring MVC, implement HandlerInterceptor: preHandle (auth, MDC requestId), postHandle, afterCompletion (timing metrics). Register via WebMvcConfigurer.addInterceptors. Differs from servlet Filter (earlier, container-wide) and from AOP (method join points).

Travel: partner API-key checks, idempotency header enforcement, audit of booking mutations.

Pitfalls: heavy I/O in preHandle; wrong order; doing business booking logic in interceptors.
mmt-be-06-012:
MVC separates Model (data), View (presentation), Controller (input/flow).

Spring MVC: DispatcherServlet front controller → maps to @Controller methods → controllers update Model and choose a view name, or @RestController writes the model as JSON via message converters (API-style “view”). Services/repositories sit behind controllers as the domain model layer.

Why: testable web layer, clear separation for booking APIs vs server-rendered pages.

Pitfall: fat controllers; assuming MVC implies JSP — REST APIs still use the MVC dispatcher pipeline.
mmt-be-06-013:
Name five with one-line intent (be ready to code 1–2):

  • Singleton: one shared instance (config/registry).
  • Factory: create objects without exposing constructors.
  • Strategy: swap algorithms (pricing) at runtime.
  • Observer: publish events; subscribers react (booking confirmed → notify).
  • State: behavior depends on lifecycle state (vending/booking).

Honorable mentions if asked: Builder, Decorator, Adapter, Circuit Breaker (resilience), Template Method.

Pitfall: listing names without a concrete production example — always tie one to MMT-style booking/payments.
mmt-be-07-001:
STAR — biggest performance win (fill metrics).

S: [Service] p99 latency ___ ms / error rate ___% under ___ QPS (e.g. hotel search or checkout).

T: Bring p99 under ___ ms and stabilize DB CPU.

A: Profiled with ___ (APM/flame graphs); found hot path ___; added Redis cache-aside / batching / index ___; bounded pools; eliminated N+1.

R: p99 ___→___ ms; QPS capacity +___%; DB load −___%. What you’d redo: ___.

Director probe: how you proved causality, rollback plan, and user impact on bookings.
mmt-be-07-002:
STAR — innovative architecture idea.

S: Team struggled with ___ (sync coupling, duplicate payment risk, slow releases).

T: Propose a change that improves reliability/velocity without big-bang rewrite.

A: Introduced ___ (outbox+Kafka, BFF, idempotency layer, contract testing, strangler facade for GDS). Built spike, RFC, got buy-in, shipped behind flag.

R: Incident rate −___%; deploy frequency +___; MTTR −___. Personal ownership: design + ___ PRs + mentoring.

Be specific why alternatives were rejected.
mmt-be-07-003:
STAR — architecture change you suggested.

S: Monolith/module X owned booking+payments; deploy risk and scaling asymmetry.

T: Split/realign boundaries or introduce async for ___ step.

A: Domain map → extract ___ service; define APIs/events; data migration plan; dual-run; feature flag cutover.

R: Independent scale of ___; deploy time ___→___; no Sev-1 during cutover / rollback used once. Lesson: ___.

Directors want trade-offs, not buzzwords — mention cost, ops burden, team ownership.
mmt-be-07-004:
STAR — Kafka design rationale.

S: Need to fan-out booking/payment outcomes to notify, loyalty, analytics without blocking checkout.

T: Reliable async propagation with clear ordering/idempotency.

A: Topics ___; key=bookingId/flightId; partitions=___; consumer groups; outbox; at-least-once + idempotent handlers; DLQ; lag alerts.

R: Checkout no longer waits on ___; lag p99 < ___ s; reprocess drill success. Why not SQS-only / why not sync REST: ___.
mmt-be-07-005:
STAR — Redis usage.
